newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-British rock band Ocean Colour Scene makes comeback.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-British rock band Ocean Colour Scene makes comeback.

text.p: When they hit the music scene in the early 1990s, British rock band Ocean Colour Scene was hailed by some as the next Rolling Stones.

This was one overnight success story that was not to be. Ocean Colour Scene quickly faded from the charts and, less than a year ago, was playing the bar circuit. But now the band is riding high again. Having sold a million copies of their latest album, "Moseley Shoals," they are expected to fill London's Royal Albert Hall on Feb. 17.
"It's come full circle," the band's lead singer, Simon Fowler, told Reuters.

Only a few years ago, it seemed like Ocean Colour Scene was set to conquer the music world. Just a few months after forming, the band signed a record deal with an independent record company !Phffft, which led to a debut single in 1990. A media frenzy hailed the group as the new Rolling Stones and even, as Fowler recalls, "everything the Beatles never were."

A record company bidding war began, leading to a deal with Fontana Records. But, despite recording tracks for the first album with Rolling Stones producer Jimmy Miller and Primal Scream producer Hugo Nicolson, Fontana rejected the tapes.
The record company drafted a third producer, Tim Palmer, known for his work with Pearl Jam, to refine the album. The end result was far from what the band had hoped for.
"The first album was released and it was welcomed by a chorus of silence," Fowler said before a recent concert at Whiskey-A-Go-Go on Hollywood's famed Sunset Strip. "It was like lard on white bread."

Relations with Fontana were further strained by the tour that followed. "By the time of the end of the tour ... we got this reputation with the record company that we were a bunch of hell-raising nutters," Fowler said.
After the tour, he said, the company refused to let the band play live, insisting they concentrate on writing for 18 months. But band members became bored and soon left the label.

Attempts to get another record deal were tough and Ocean Colour Scene was rejected by at least 18 companies before eventually linking up with MCA Records late last year. Meanwhile the band's financial troubles grew and with legal costs and other expenses spiraling Chris Cradock, father of guitarist Steve Cradock and band manager, took out a second mortgage on his house and eventually had to sell it.

Salvation came in the form of Paul Weller, the Godfather of the English "Mod" scene. Steve Cradock landed a job as guitarist with Weller, who was once again topping the charts. Soon all four members of the band were helping Weller out.

"It was a real buoyancy that Weller gave the band, it gave us confidence and also it gave us so much fun. And financially Steve would keep our studio going by using the money he was paid," Fowler said. "The whole thing was a blessing."

The band began recording what was to become their "Moseley Shoals" album as demo tapes to get a recording deal and soon reached a deal with MCA Records. Since then the album, launched by the hypnotic "Riverboat Song," has reached near triple-platinum status in England with almost 900,000 units sold and four hit singles.

One of the high points of the year for the band was playing in front of more than 100,000 at the Loch Lomond summer festival in Scotland. And people are still comparing them to the Rolling Stones. "I feel quite good about that," Fowler said. "It's better than being compared to Bon Jovi."
With the band riding the crest of a wave, Chris Cradock, whose unswerving faith in his son's band led to the loss of his house, was recently able to buy another one, Fowler said.
